parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Give each principle an observable meaning
parts.body:
The OECD AI Principles address inclusive growth; human rights, fairness, and privacy; transparency; robustness, security, and safety; and accountability. They are intergovernmental principles, updated in 2024, rather than a product certification or a substitute for local law. A CAIO should ask what each principle requires in a specific workflow and what evidence would show whether it is working.

For a customer-facing advice assistant, transparency could mean telling users when they interact with AI, presenting the source and limits of an answer, and providing a route to a person. Fairness might require checking whether service quality differs by language, accessibility need, or customer segment. Accountability requires a named owner who can correct harm and change the process. The required controls vary by use, not by a single enterprise slogan.

Put a principle-to-control table in the use record. For each principle, describe a possible harm, preventive or detective control, test method, owner, and escalation threshold. Some values can conflict: a highly detailed explanation may reveal protected information, while aggressive data collection to measure fairness may increase privacy risk. Make the tradeoff explicit and have the responsible specialists review it.

example.title: A fairness question with an owner
example.body: A multilingual benefits assistant answers in English and French. The service owner samples equivalent questions in both languages and tracks correction rates. If French responses omit eligibility caveats more often, pause the affected answer path and repair its sources before extending usage.

exercise.title: Translate two principles
exercise.body: Choose a use case and write two rows, each with a principle, a person who could be harmed, control, evidence, owner, and stop trigger. Explain a tradeoff between the rows and who decides it.

parts.label: Design
parts.title: Make human oversight real
parts.body:
A person placed after a model output is not automatically an effective control. The reviewer must know the task, see relevant evidence, have time to examine it, and have authority to reject or change the recommendation. Measure whether reviewers actually spot important errors under ordinary workload. If the system's confidence display encourages automatic agreement, test that behavior too.

Decide which outcomes require human authorization, which can be reversed, and which must never be automated. Record handoff rules, escalation, and appeal channels. A high-volume service team may need a sampled quality review for low-impact drafts and item-by-item approval for consequential actions. The relevant legal regime may impose additional specific requirements; the design team should not infer legal sufficiency from the presence of a reviewer.

Give operators a way to report failure without blame and a clear route to pause use. Train them on limits and excluded cases. Review override rates alongside quality: a low rate could mean good performance or could mean reviewers stopped checking. Interview operators and sample cases before drawing a conclusion.

example.title: A loan explanation draft
example.body: An assistant drafts an explanation of a declined application using verified decision reasons supplied by the lender. An authorized employee compares it with the actual decision record and can rewrite or reject it. Quality review checks for invented reasons and whether customer challenges reach the appropriate team; counsel maps the applicable credit and privacy rules.

exercise.title: Test a reviewer
exercise.body: Give three reviewers a set of 20 illustrative outputs with two known consequential errors, realistic time pressure, and access to source material. Record detection, corrections, and time. Decide whether to improve the interface, add training, narrow scope, or stop use.

sources: OECD AI Principles: human oversight and transparency
NIST AI RMF Core: human-AI configuration

parts.label: Measure
parts.title: Check distribution of benefit and harm
parts.body:
An average improvement can conceal a worse experience for a smaller group. Start with the process baseline and identify whose outcomes could change. Choose slices justified by the use and permitted by applicable privacy, employment, and anti-discrimination law. Inspect error severity and opportunity to contest a result, not only mean accuracy. Where group data cannot be collected, document the limit and use other lawful methods, such as targeted usability work or qualitative feedback.

A service assistant may improve average resolution time while consistently failing on one language or accessibility path. Measure response quality, abandonment, escalations, and complaints across channels. Keep denominators and uncertainty visible; a difference from five cases is a signal to investigate, not proof of a stable population effect. Engage people who use and experience the service where feasible.

The executive choice is whether the observed tradeoff warrants narrower deployment, more data collection, better service design, or discontinuation. State what improvement is required before expansion and who can authorize it. Recheck after changes, because a revised model or knowledge base can redistribute errors.

example.title: An aggregate score hides a gap
example.body: In an illustrative pilot, overall correct answers improve from 80% to 87%, but French-language answers fall from 82% to 74%. The service owner holds French rollout, inspects retrieval sources and tests a corrected version. The figures are hypothetical and do not imply a universal fairness threshold.

exercise.title: Write a disaggregated scorecard
exercise.body: Pick an AI-supported service. Name the baseline, meaningful slices, minimum sample or uncertainty display, severity categories, and an escalation route. Add a method for affected users to report an error and a decision date for expansion.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: MAP and MEASURE

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Resolve a principle conflict in an executive forum
parts.body:
Principles are most useful when they change a decision. Suppose a health service wants to log full conversations to investigate harmful answers. Detailed logs aid safety investigations, but sensitive personal information creates retention and access risk. Ask which fields investigators actually need, whether redaction works, who may read logs, and how long they are needed. Privacy and security teams should assess the proposed design under the relevant law.

Present at least two viable options with expected benefit, residual harm, evidence, cost, and owner. One option might keep short-lived, restricted transcripts with audited access. Another might keep redacted excerpts and event metadata, escalating only serious cases for fuller preservation under a defined process. Test whether the second option still permits investigation. Do not claim that one setting is lawful everywhere.

Record the chosen boundary, dissent or unresolved uncertainty, and a date for review. Follow up with incidents and user feedback. Responsible AI practice requires correction when the control fails, not merely an ethics statement at procurement.

example.title: A bounded logging choice
example.body: The executive approves redacted logs for routine quality review, with a restricted incident-preservation process for serious events. Privacy and security specialists verify access, retention, and transfer terms in the relevant jurisdictions. The service owner reviews whether investigators can still reconstruct failures.

exercise.title: Chair a decision
exercise.body: Write a five-minute decision brief for the logging case: affected people, options, evidence gap, recommendation, accountable executive, and trigger to revisit. Include what you would ask a Canadian privacy adviser and an EU GDPR adviser.

sources: Canadian privacy regulators: principles for generative AI
European Data Protection Board: AI models and GDPR opinion
